strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors (VLODs). The paper makes a reasonable case that existing VLM TTA methods (designed for classification) are not directly applicable to detection, where predictions come from many proposals coupled with localization.

The IoU-weighted Entropy Minimization (IWE) component is well-motivated and technically sensible. Exploiting the dense proposal structure of detectors as free test-time augmentation, and down-weighting isolated/misaligned boxes via class-specific IoU graph components, is a clean idea that is clearly illustrated in Figs. 1 and 11.

The Image-Conditioned Prompt Selection (IPS) component is well-justified by the empirical observation (Fig. 2) that standard prompt averaging can degrade VLOD performance; selecting top-ρ prompts by image-level similarity is a reasonable alternative to uniform ensembling.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 main datasets (Watercolor, ClipArt, Comic, Cityscapes, BDD100K, ExDark) plus Pascal-C and COCO-C across 15 corruptions, with four adapted TTA baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, Adapter), and results on two distinct detector architectures (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO) and two model sizes (Table 5).

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analysis: effect of θ, γ, λ, ρ (Fig. 6), prompt-generation strategy (Fig. 4), adapter placement (Fig. 5), top-M proposals (Fig. 8), batch size and augmentation (Fig. 10), and fine-tuning before adaptation (Tables 6-7).
Good engineering transparency: complexity/latency and parameter budget reported (Table 3), with a fair comparison against baselines that also require backpropagation.
Clear writing, informative motivation figures, and a well-organized presentation.
weaknesses: The magnitude of improvements is modest in several settings. For example, on BDD100K (YOLO-World), VLOD-TTA improves over the Adapter baseline by only +0.9 mAP; on ExDark (GD), the improvement over Adapter is +0.3 AP50. The paper claims "significant" improvements in the conclusion, which overstates the effect sizes for the strongest baselines.

Technical novelty of the individual components is limited. IWE is essentially a reweighting of standard marginal entropy minimization, and IPS is closely related to prompt ensembling/selection techniques already established in the VLM-TTA literature. The contribution is primarily an adaptation/combination of known ideas to a new setting rather than a fundamentally new method.

The "first TTA framework for VLODs" claim deserves more scrutiny. The related work acknowledges Medeiros et al. (2025) adapts VLODs across modalities but in a supervised setting; the distinction (unsupervised TTA) should be stated more carefully and contrasted explicitly rather than asserted in a single sentence.

Computational overhead is non-trivial: 20 FPS vs 89 FPS for zero-shot (Table 3), i.e., ~4.5× slower, due to a per-image backward pass and IoU graph construction. Given the TTA setting, this cost may limit practical deployment, and the paper does not discuss real-time or streaming constraints.

Reliance on GPT-generated prompts for IPS, computed offline for YOLO-World, introduces an external model dependency. It is unclear how sensitive results are to the prompt-generation model, and dataset-agnostic prompts are reported to underperform dataset-specific ones (Fig. 4), which raises questions about generalizability.
No variance/statistical significance is reported across runs or seeds. Given the small margins over strong baselines in several settings, confidence intervals would materially affect the conclusions.

The "Code :" line in the abstract is empty, raising reproducibility concerns at review time. The paper does not describe hyperparameter selection protocol (e.g., how γ, λ, ρ were tuned without a validation set), which is important for a TTA method claiming to work with unlabeled target data only.

The limitation that IWE underperforms on scenes with many tiny low-overlap objects (e.g., Cityscapes) is acknowledged but not resolved; the paper could have explored alternative objectives or an adaptive γ to address this.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and under-explored problem: test-time adaptation specifically for vision-language object detectors (VLODs). The authors make a reasonable case that TTA methods designed for classification (entropy minimization, prompt tuning, cache-based) are not directly suitable for detection, and the framing of the contribution as the first TTA framework for VLODs is well-motivated and supported by the related work section.

The two proposed components are conceptually clean and well-justified. IoU-weighted Entropy Minimization (IWE) exploits the spatial redundancy of dense proposals by weighting each proposal by the size of its same-class IoU-connected component, and Image-conditioned Prompt Selection (IPS) avoids the pitfalls of uniform prompt averaging, which the authors convincingly show can degrade detection performance. Both motivations are illustrated with clear figures (Figs. 1 and 2).

The experimental evaluation is extensive and thorough: 6 benchmark datasets (Watercolor, ClipArt, Comic, Cityscapes, BDD100K, ExDark) plus Pascal-C and COCO-C across 15 corruption types and 5 severity levels, yielding a large set of test scenarios. Results are reported for both a CNN-based detector (YOLO-World) and a transformer-based detector (Grounding DINO), and additionally for larger backbones (YOLO-World-L, Grounding DINO-B), demonstrating architecture-agnostic applicability.

Ablations and analyses are detailed and informative: prompt-generation strategies, adapter placement per module, sensitivity to all four key hyperparameters (θ, γ, λ, ρ), effect of top-M proposals, batch size, augmentations, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning. The complexity analysis (Table 3, FPS and trainable parameter counts) provides a useful robustness/cost trade-off perspective and shows the method is competitive with or faster than several TTA baselines.

Methodological details are mostly well specified (adapter configurations, zero-initialization, single adaptation step, weight detachment during backprop), which supports reproducibility, and the limitations section candidly notes where the method underperforms (tiny, low-overlap objects in Cityscapes).
weaknesses: The absolute performance gains are modest in several regimes (e.g., ~+1.0 to +3.3 mAP/AP50 on style shifts, and smaller gains on driving scenes and some COCO-C corruptions). On COCO-C the paper itself acknowledges that standard entropy minimization occasionally outperforms the proposed method on specific corruptions and that all baselines degrade severely at higher severities, which somewhat limits the practical significance of the reported improvements.

The IoU threshold θ is selected differently per dataset (≈0.7 for Watercolor, ≈0.5 for ClipArt/Comic), and the fusion coefficient λ differs substantially between YOLO-World (0.3) and Grounding DINO (0.1). Since TTA presumes no access to target-domain labels, this dataset-dependent tuning raises a legitimate concern about how θ and λ would be set in a truly label-free deployment; the sensitivity analysis mitigates but does not fully resolve this.

IWE constructs weights from the detector's own predicted classes and IoU overlaps, so the objective still depends on the model's potentially biased initial predictions. The paper argues that spatial coherence reduces confirmation bias, but a more direct analysis of when this assumption fails (e.g., systematically misclassified but spatially dense proposals) would strengthen the claim.

The prompt pool for IPS relies on GPT-generated prompts, introducing an external model dependency at (or before) adaptation time. While the paper states embeddings are computed offline for YOLO-World, the practical cost and reproducibility implications of this dependency, and whether a simple hand-crafted synonym pool would suffice, are not fully explored.

The reported code link in the abstract is empty ("Code :"), which is a minor but noticeable presentation issue. More broadly, the method adds a backward pass at inference and an IoU-graph construction step; while Table 3 shows this is acceptable relative to baselines, the latency overhead relative to zero-shot is non-trivial for real-time VLODs like YOLO-World.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant setting — unsupervised test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors (VLODs) — and frames the gap clearly, with a plausible (if narrowly drawn) claim to being the first such framework.

The empirical study is unusually thorough for a paper of this scope: six target datasets spanning style, driving, and low-light shift, plus 15 corruption types on PASCAL-C and COCO-C, evaluated on two architecturally different VLODs (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), with appendix results for larger backbones, batch size, and augmentation.

The IoU-weighted entropy objective (IWE) is a sensible, detector-specific use of the dense, overlapping proposal structure that detectors naturally produce, and the motivating observation (standard entropy sharpens isolated/mislabeled proposals indiscriminately) is well illustrated in Fig. 1.

Ablations are informative and go beyond the minimum: adapter placement per module, effect of top-M proposals, prompt-averaging vs. prompt-selection, and hyperparameter sensitivity are all probed, and the throughput/parameter comparison (Table 3) usefully positions the cost of the method.

Improvements over zero-shot are consistent across nearly all datasets and corruption families, with the clearest and largest gains for the more complex Grounding DINO model (e.g., +3.3 mAP on Cityscapes), and the writing and organization are clear enough to be reproduced.
The paper is candid about one limitation (IWE can underperform in scenes dominated by many tiny, low-overlap objects such as Cityscapes), which strengthens rather than weakens the scientific case.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. IWE is essentially standard entropy minimization (TENT) with a cluster-size weighting applied to the loss, and IPS is a top-ρ prompt-selection scheme; both are simple modifications of existing ideas, and no theoretical analysis is given for why cluster-size weighting should improve calibration rather than merely rescale gradients toward large proposal groups.

Gains over the closest and strongest baseline (Adapter, i.e., TENT applied to adapters) are small and often near noise. On YOLO-World, the improvement attributable to IWE+IPS over Adapter is only ~+0.6 to +2.0 mAP (e.g., +0.6 on ExDark and Comic, +1.1 on Cityscapes, +0.9 on BDD100K), meaning the headline improvements largely stem from simply adding adapters rather than from the proposed contributions.

The core mechanism constructs the IoU graph on predicted class labels ĉ_i derived from the very scores being sharpened, so it risks reinforcing erroneous proposal clusters — precisely the confirmation-bias pathology the paper criticizes in standard entropy minimization. This failure mode is not systematically quantified; the supporting qualitative evidence (Fig. 1, Fig. 11) is anecdotal and appears selected to show cases where the dominant cluster is correct, with no measurement of how often the largest cluster is the wrong class.

No comparison is made to the recent object-detection TTA methods the paper itself cites (STFAR, Cao et al. 2025, Ruan & Tang 2024). The claim that these are inapplicable to VLODs because they 'rely on heavy augmentations and multi-step updates' is asserted rather than demonstrated, so superiority over the broader TTA literature is not established.

The method introduces several new hyperparameters (γ, θ, ρ, λ, and M) whose optimal values vary across datasets (Fig. 6, Fig. 8), which undercuts the 'adapt on the fly without tuning' promise of TTA; the reported defaults may not be optimal for unseen target domains.

The 'first TTA framework for VLODs' claim is strong given that the method reduces largely to TENT-with-adapters plus prompt selection, and the boundary to prior work (e.g., the supervised VLOD adaptation of Medeiros et al. 2025) is drawn narrowly.

Reproducibility is weakened by the blank code link in the abstract and by the use of GPT-generated prompt pools for which only illustrative examples (Table 4) are provided, making exact replication of the prompt-selection component difficult.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors. The proposed VLOD-TTA is practical and well motivated, with two intuitive components: IoU-weighted entropy minimization (IWE) to exploit proposal redundancy, and image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) to avoid uninformative prompt averaging.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: six benchmark datasets and 15 corruption types, covering style shifts, driving conditions, low-light, and common corruptions, with two representative VLOD backbones (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO). The ablation studies are thorough and isolate the contributions of IWE, IPS, adapter placement, prompt design, batch size, and input resolution.

The comparison with the prior VLOD TTA method, TTAOD-F, highlights a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off: VLOD-TTA obtains slightly better or comparable accuracy with far lower GPU memory and latency, which is important for practical deployment. The paper also includes failure-case analysis on Cityscapes and specialized-domain evaluation on Aquarium.

The method is simple and computationally lightweight, requiring only a single adaptation step and a small set of trainable adapter/residual parameters. This makes it more deployable than teacher-based or multi-step TTA methods, and the paper provides hyperparameter sensitivity analyses that support stability across datasets.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and reports implementation details and supplementary analyses that improve reproducibility. The limitations are acknowledged, including reduced effectiveness on scenes with many small objects and slower-than-zero-shot inference due to gradient-based adaptation.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate. Both IWE and IPS are relatively straightforward adaptations of existing ideas: entropy minimization reweighted by proposal overlap, and prompt selection instead of prompt averaging. The contribution is primarily in the application and empirical validation for VLODs rather than in fundamentally new methodology.

The IPS compatibility score averages prompt-region similarities over all proposals in the image rather than restricting to proposals predicted as the target class. This can make prompt selection less class-specific than intended, since prompts are ranked by global image-level compatibility rather than by alignment with confident class-specific regions. The paper could better justify or ablate this design choice.

Absolute gains are modest in several settings, especially on structured driving datasets such as Cityscapes and BDD100K, where improvements over zero-shot are small. Statistical significance is not reported, so the robustness of small average gains is unclear.

Hyperparameter selection is not fully transparent. The main experiments use fixed values, but it is not clearly stated whether these were chosen using target-domain labels or validation splits. This matters because TTA methods should not tune on the target test distribution, and the paper would benefit from a clearer protocol.

The TTAOD-F comparison is limited to COCO-C with Grounding DINO. Since TTAOD-F is the most relevant prior method, a broader comparison, including PASCAL-C or style-shift datasets, would strengthen the claim. The reproduction relies on proprietary GPT-generated prompts, which could hinder exact reproducibility.

strengths: The paper tackles an underexplored and practically important problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors. It identifies concrete failure modes of standard entropy minimization and prompt averaging in VLODs and proposes targeted components (IWE and IPS).

IWE is well motivated by the observation that VLODs produce dense, overlapping proposals, and it incorporates spatial coherence via an IoU graph and connected-component weighting. IPS replaces uniform prompt averaging with image-conditioned prompt selection, and both components are ablated thoroughly.

The empirical study is extensive: six benchmark datasets, fifteen corruption types, two representative VLODs, multiple adapted TTA baselines, sensitivity analyses, qualitative results, and efficiency comparisons. The gains are consistent across stylized, driving, low-light, and corruption benchmarks, and the method is substantially more efficient than the prior TTAOD-F in parameters, latency, and GPU memory.

The paper is generally clear, with detailed implementation settings, adapter configurations, hyperparameter choices, prompt examples, and supplement providing additional analysis. Limitations (e.g., Cityscapes small-object failures, latency overhead) are acknowledged.

The contribution is timely and likely useful to practitioners deploying open-vocabulary detectors under distribution shift, especially because it avoids a teacher model and supports both CNN- and transformer-based VLODs.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: IWE and IPS are intuitive combinations of existing ideas (entropy minimization, IoU-based clustering, prompt ensembling/selection). The core improvement is engineering-driven, and the reported gains over strong baselines are often incremental, even if consistent.

IPS computes prompt compatibility scores by averaging over all region proposals, including many background or irrelevant boxes. This can bias prompt selection toward image-dominant classes, introduce noise for rare or absent classes, and lacks strong theoretical justification beyond a trivial cosine-Euclidean equivalence. Filtering proposals by predicted class or confidence before prompt scoring would be more principled.

IWE weights depend on predicted labels and top-M proposals, so groups of false positives with high mutual overlap could still receive large weights. The Cityscapes analysis shows failure cases with label overlap (rider/person) and small objects, suggesting the method can reinforce annotation/confusion biases under certain conditions.

Evaluation is limited to YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, with main experiments on small/tiny variants. Although the supplement includes larger backbones and a specialized aquarium domain, broader detector and architecture diversity is still limited. TTAOD-F, the most relevant prior method, is compared only on COCO-C in the main paper, with limited comparison across the full set of domain shifts.

Reproducibility and rigor could be strengthened: the code link is empty/placeholder, prompt generation relies on ChatGPT-5 without releasing the full prompt pool or a fixed deterministic set, and no error bars or repeated-run statistics are reported. Test-time single-image adaptation can have high variance, so significance of the reported gains is unclear.

strengths: Addresses the underexplored and timely problem of test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), where prior work is scarce and mostly limited to a high-overhead teacher-based method.

The proposed IWE objective is well motivated by the failure of standard entropy minimization under dense, overlapping object proposals; using IoU graph cluster size to reweight entropy is simple, efficient, and conceptually sensible.
The IPS prompt-selection module replaces uniform prompt averaging with image-conditioned prompt selection, and the ablation shows it can avoid cases where prompt averaging harms detection confidence.

Evaluation is broad and thorough: six benchmark datasets, 15 common corruption types, multiple detectors (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO), backbone variations, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples.

Efficiency analysis is a clear practical strength: compared with the prior TTAOD-F, the method uses far fewer tunable parameters and substantially lower GPU memory and latency, supporting deployment-oriented claims.
The paper is generally well written and well illustrated; the motivation figures and qualitative visualizations help explain the design choices.
The authors include a failure-case analysis (e.g., Cityscapes label overlap and small objects) and additional empirical studies, which is a positive step toward transparent evaluation.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: IWE is a heuristic entropy reweighting scheme based on proposal cluster size, and IPS is an image-conditioned top-k prompt selection mechanism; neither contributes a substantially new learning principle or theoretical insight for VLOD adaptation.

Empirical gains over the strongest adapter/standard-entropy baselines are often small and inconsistent. Several ablation improvements are only 0.2–1.0 mAP, and no statistical significance or variance is reported, making it difficult to claim a robust advance.

The comparison with the only prior VLOD TTA method, TTAOD-F, is marginal in accuracy: without warm-start initialization, VLOD-TTA obtains only a 0.2 mAP average advantage on COCO-C. The clearest advantage is efficiency, not adaptation quality; the warm-start variant also borrows an initialization strategy from the prior method.

The TTA setting is somewhat unconventional: the method resets trainable parameters after every test image and performs only a single adaptation step per image. This prevents online accumulation and is closer to per-image test-time optimization than to standard online TTA, weakening the framing and comparison.

IWE can reinforce confirmation bias when a large but incorrect proposal cluster exists. The authors’ own Cityscapes analysis shows degraded rider/person behavior, but no method-level remedy is proposed beyond changing annotation granularity or input resolution.

The open-vocabulary setting assumes a known target-domain class prompt pool. It is unclear how the method behaves when the target label set is unknown, incomplete, or contains out-of-distribution categories, which is a core practical scenario for VLODs.

Several baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE) are adapted from vision-language classification TTA to object detection; they may not be optimal for detection. Comparisons are further limited to a small number of detectors and lack error bars or significance testing.

Reproducibility is weakened by a missing/blank code link in the abstract, and some implementation details remain deferred to the supplementary material, including exact prompt-generation procedures and IWE graph threshold behavior.
